reference_title: Ground Modification Methods Reference Manual – Volume I

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduction to the aggregate columns chapter (p. 5-1): describes the technology, its history, the focus and scope of the technical summary, the primary references and related cement-based column technologies (VCCs and CMCs).
sections.body: Chapter 5 opens (p. 5-1) with the introduction to aggregate columns, a ground modification technique that covers both stone columns and rammed aggregate piers. The introduction is organized into the description and history of the technology (Section 1.1), a historical overview (1.2), the focus and scope of the technical summary (1.3), the primary references (1.4) and related technologies such as vibro-concrete columns and controlled modulus columns (1.5).
key_points: Aggregate columns include stone columns and rammed aggregate piers (p. 5-1).
sections.applicability: Orientation to the chapter on aggregate column ground modification.

sections.title: Description and History
sections.summary: Aggregate columns have become established in the United States over the past 30 years as a ground modification technique for transportation facilities; they are ideally suited for clays, silts, loose silty sands and uncompacted fills (p. 5-1).
sections.body: Over the past 30 years aggregate column technology has become established in the United States as a viable ground modification technique and has been applied extensively for remediation and new construction of transportation facilities (p. 5-1). Conventional embankment construction methods such as preloading, dredging and soil displacement can often no longer be used because of environmental restrictions and post-construction maintenance expenses. Aggregate columns have a proven record of experience and are ideally suited for use in clays, silts, loose silty sands and uncompacted fills. The section introduces the history and development of aggregate columns, the focus and scope of the technical summary and the primary references.
key_points: Ideally suited for clays, silts, loose silty sands and uncompacted fills (p. 5-1).
Used where preloading, dredging or soil displacement are restricted by environmental or maintenance concerns.
sections.applicability: Screening whether aggregate columns suit a soft-ground transportation project.

sections.title: Description
sections.summary: Defines the term aggregate columns as covering both rammed aggregate piers and stone columns; where an attribute applies to only one type the specific column type is named (p. 5-1).
sections.body: The technical summary on aggregate columns includes both rammed aggregate piers and stone columns, and their similarities and differences are presented in the following sections (p. 5-1). When an attribute applies to both stone columns and rammed aggregate piers the manual uses the term aggregate columns. When an attribute is specific to only one of the two types, the column is identified as a stone column or a rammed aggregate pier.
key_points: 'Aggregate columns' = stone columns plus rammed aggregate piers (p. 5-1).
sections.applicability: Terminology used throughout Chapter 5.

sections.title: Stone Columns
sections.summary: Stone columns are built by down-hole vibratory methods that introduce backfill to form dense, interlocked columns; the two techniques are vibro-replacement (wet, top feed) and vibro-displacement (dry, top or bottom feed) (pp. 5-1 to 5-2).
sections.body: Stone column construction is accomplished by down-hole vibratory methods (p. 5-1). Backfill material is introduced into the soil so that dense and sometimes deep columns of aggregate are formed, tightly interlocked with the surrounding soil. The technique is known as either vibro-replacement or vibro-displacement. Vibro-replacement generally refers to the wet, top feed process, in which jetting water aids penetration of the vibrator; part of the in situ soil is washed to the surface and replaced by the backfill (e.g. stone). A dry feed process with soils requiring predrilling also brings in situ soil to the surface. Vibro-displacement generally refers to the dry, top or bottom feed process; almost no in situ soil appears at the surface, as it is displaced by the backfill. The product of both methods is generically referred to as a stone column (p. 5-2).
key_points: Vibro-replacement: wet, top feed; jetting water washes part of the in situ soil to the surface (p. 5-1).
Vibro-displacement: dry, top or bottom feed; soil is displaced, almost none reaches the surface (p. 5-1).
Both methods produce what is generically called a stone column (p. 5-2).
sections.applicability: Distinguishing the wet and dry stone column installation methods.

sections.title: Rammed Aggregate Piers
sections.summary: Rammed aggregate piers are formed by drilling 18- to 36-inch holes, typically 7 to 33 ft deep, and ramming lifts of well-graded aggregate with a beveled tamper to form stiff, high-density columns (p. 5-2).
sections.body: Rammed aggregate piers are installed by drilling 18- to 36-inch diameter holes into the foundation soils and ramming lifts of well-graded aggregate within the holes to form stiff, high-density aggregate columns (p. 5-2). The drilled holes typically extend from 7 to 33 feet below grade. The first lift of aggregate forms a bulb below the bottom of the pier, and subsequent lifts are typically 12 inches thick. Ramming is done with a high-energy beveled tamper that both densifies the aggregate and forces it laterally into the sidewalls of the hole. This increases the lateral stress in the surrounding soil, further stiffening the stabilized composite soil mass.
key_points: Hole diameter 18 to 36 inches; depth typically 7 to 33 ft (p. 5-2).
First lift forms a bottom bulb; subsequent lifts typically 12 inches (p. 5-2).
Ramming increases lateral stress in the surrounding soil (p. 5-2).
sections.applicability: Describing rammed aggregate pier construction for design and specification.

sections.title: Historical Overview
sections.summary: History of deep vibratory methods from vibro-compaction (1936) to stone columns and rammed aggregate piers; Figure 5-1 shows the grain size ranges applicable to vibro-compaction and stone columns (pp. 5-2 to 5-3).
sections.body: Deep vibrators have been used for over 50 years to improve the bearing resistance and settlement performance of weak soils (p. 5-2). As early as 1936 methods and equipment allowed compaction of non-cohesive soils to depths of 60 feet; this process is now called vibro-compaction or vibro-flotation. Stone columns developed as a natural progression that extended vibro-systems beyond densification of clean granular soils (Figure 5-1). Soils whose grain size curves lie entirely on the coarse side of the hatched line in Figure 5-1 are readily compacted by vibro-compaction; soils whose curves fall to the right of the dotted line are not, and these soils led to stone column technology (p. 5-3). One of the first documented uses of stone columns was a historic structure completed in 1653 on hand-dug pits backfilled with stone; the concept was used in France in the 1830s (FHWA 1983), modern techniques began in Europe in the 1960s, and the technique reached the United States in the 1970s with only 21 projects in its first 12 years but over 400 by 1994. Rammed aggregate piers were developed in the United States in 1984 and refined over the last 25 years under a trade name; they are installed in 2 to 3 foot diameter holes 7 to 33 feet deep with well-graded or open graded aggregate.
key_points: Vibro-compaction dates from 1936, to depths of 60 ft (p. 5-2).
Figure 5-1: soils coarse of the hatched line are readily vibro-compacted; finer soils led to stone columns (p. 5-3).
Stone column use in the US: 21 projects in the first 12 years, over 400 by 1994 (p. 5-3).
Rammed aggregate piers developed in the US in 1984 (p. 5-3).
figures: Figure 5-1: Soils applicable for stone columns.
sections.applicability: Background on where vibro-compaction stops and stone columns apply by grain size.

sections.title: Focus and Scope
sections.summary: States that the technical summary gives guidance on applications, design, contracting methods and quality assurance for aggregate columns, with references for detail and typical costs for preliminary technical and economic evaluation (p. 5-3).
sections.body: The focus and scope of the technical summary on aggregate columns is to provide guidance on applications where the technology can be used, design, contracting methods and quality assurance (p. 5-3). References are cited where more detailed technical information can be obtained, and typical costs are given so that a preliminary technical and economic evaluation can be made of whether aggregate columns and related technologies are appropriate for a site and application. The document is intended to serve as a reference on aggregate columns and how they may best be used on a ground modification project, by discussing their construction, use and limitations.
key_points: Covers applications, design, contracting methods and quality assurance (p. 5-3).
sections.applicability: Defines what the chapter does and does not cover.

sections.title: Primary References
sections.summary: Lists the two primary references for the chapter: FHWA (1983) Design and Construction of Stone Columns (Barksdale and Bachus) and Collin (2007), the HITEC evaluation of rammed aggregate piers (p. 5-4).
sections.body: The primary references for aggregate columns are listed on p. 5-4: FHWA (1983), Design and Construction of Stone Columns, by Barksdale and Bachus, FHWA/RD-83/026, Volumes I and II; and Collin (2007), the technical evaluation report on rammed aggregate piers prepared by the Highway Innovative Technology Evaluation Center (HITEC), ASCE, 86 p.
key_points: FHWA (1983), Barksdale and Bachus, FHWA/RD-83/026 (p. 5-4).
Collin (2007), HITEC evaluation report on rammed aggregate piers (p. 5-4).
sections.applicability: Where to find the detailed design background for stone columns and rammed aggregate piers.

sections.title: Related Technologies
sections.summary: Related column technologies, many proprietary, use Portland cement binder or concrete to build stiffer columns; the two common cement based columns are vibro-concrete columns (VCCs) and controlled modulus columns (CMCs) (p. 5-4).
sections.body: A variety of column technologies are related and similar to aggregate columns (p. 5-4). Many are proprietary technologies developed by ground modification contractors; some are equipment and installation variations better suited to particular conditions, such as installation below the water table or in very soft soils. Many use a Portland cement binder with the aggregate, producing a more rigid (cemented aggregate) column, and another option is to build the column of concrete. Two common cement based columns are vibro-concrete columns (VCCs) and controlled modulus columns (CMCs). Cement based concrete columns may be used in softer soils, without casing, and give a stiffer element than aggregate columns.
key_points: Cement based columns (VCCs, CMCs) give stiffer elements and can be used in softer soils without casing (p. 5-4).
sections.applicability: Choosing between aggregate columns and cement based column alternatives in very soft soils.

sections.title: Vibro-Concrete Columns
sections.summary: VCCs replace the stone with concrete pumped through a bottom feed vibrator, forming an enlarged base and a continuous shaft; developed in Europe in 1976 for very soft clay or peat and first used in the US in 1994 (pp. 5-4 to 5-5).
sections.body: Vibro-concrete columns (VCC) are a sister technology to stone columns with concrete replacing the stone (p. 5-4). The non-proprietary process uses a vibro-displacement (bottom feed) depth vibrator to penetrate to a suitable bearing level. Concrete is pumped through the vibrator during initial withdrawal; the vibrator then re-penetrates the concrete, displacing it to form an enlarged base, and is slowly withdrawn while concrete is pumped at a maintained pressure to form a continuous shaft to ground level, where a slight mushroom assists load transfer. VCCs were first developed in Europe in 1976 because stone column capacity is significantly reduced in very soft clay or peat thicker than 1 to 2 column diameters. They combine the ground modification advantages of vibro-systems with the load carrying characteristics of a deep foundation (p. 5-5). The first US installation was in 1994 for an oil storage tank, and VCCs have supported embankments over soft organic soils in several states. GeoTechTools gives detailed guidance.
key_points: Stone column capacity is significantly reduced in very soft clay or peat thicker than 1 to 2 column diameters; VCCs were developed for these soils (p. 5-4).
First US installation 1994 (p. 5-5).
sections.applicability: Considering a concrete column where soft organic layers are too thick for stone columns.

sections.title: Controlled Modulus Columns
sections.summary: CMCs are proprietary, patented concrete columns built with a reverse displacement auger that pumps low slump concrete through its hollow stem; developed in France in the early 1990s and introduced in the USA and Canada in 2003 (p. 5-5).
sections.body: Controlled modulus columns (CMCs) are produced with a proprietary process and, like VCCs, the final product is a concrete column (p. 5-5). They are constructed with a reverse auger that displaces the site soil until an adequate bearing layer is reached; low slump concrete is pumped through the hollow stem as the auger is withdrawn. CMCs are a patented technology. The technique was developed in the early 1990s in France by a specialty contractor, which designed machines and tooling that let it grow rapidly in Europe, and it was introduced in the USA and Canada in 2003, the first project supporting a retail store.
key_points: CMCs use a displacement auger and low slump concrete pumped through the hollow stem (p. 5-5).
Patented technology, introduced in North America in 2003 (p. 5-5).
sections.applicability: Background on a proprietary concrete column alternative to aggregate columns.

sections.title: Design and Construction Considerations of VCCs and CMCs
sections.summary: Feasibility factors for VCCs and CMCs: allowable load depends on diameter, concrete strength and bearing layer; diameters 18-24 in. (VCC) and 10-18 in. (CMC); allowable loads 150-250 kips and 75-150 kips; lengths 20 to 75 ft (p. 5-5).
sections.body: A generalized summary of factors affecting feasibility of stabilizing soft ground with VCCs and CMCs is given on p. 5-5. (1) The allowable design load is a function of column diameter, allowable concrete strength and the strength of the bearing layer. Typical diameters are 18 to 24 inches for VCCs and 10 to 18 inches for CMCs; typical allowable design loads are 150 to 250 kips for VCCs and 75 to 150 kips for CMCs. (2) VCCs and CMCs are typically used in very soft clay and organic soils. (3) Typical lengths vary from 20 to 75 feet. GeoTechTools gives information on design, specification, quality assurance and construction of VCCs, which also guides other cement based column technologies.
key_points: VCC diameter 18-24 in., allowable load 150-250 kips (p. 5-5).
CMC diameter 10-18 in., allowable load 75-150 kips (p. 5-5).
Typical lengths 20 to 75 ft; used in very soft clay and organic soils (p. 5-5).
sections.applicability: Preliminary sizing and feasibility of VCCs and CMCs.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Aggregate column construction partially replaces or displaces unsuitable subsurface soil with a vertical column of compacted aggregate; the section covers applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility, limitations and alternatives (p. 5-6).
sections.body: Aggregate column construction involves the partial replacement or displacement of unsuitable subsurface soils with a vertical column of compacted aggregate (p. 5-6). Section 2.0 discusses applications, advantages and disadvantages, and design considerations for aggregate columns, including feasibility evaluations (geotechnical, environmental, site), limitations and alternative modification methods.
key_points: Aggregate columns partially replace or displace unsuitable soil with compacted aggregate (p. 5-6).
sections.applicability: Deciding whether aggregate columns are a candidate ground modification method.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Aggregate columns increase bearing resistance, reduce total and differential settlement, accelerate settlement, improve slope stability and reduce liquefaction potential; applications include highways, embankments, warehouses and light industrial buildings (p. 5-6).
sections.body: Aggregate columns can be applied to increase bearing resistance, reduce total and differential settlements, accelerate the time rate of settlement, improve slope stability and reduce the liquefaction potential of soil (p. 5-6). Typical applications include foundation improvement for construction of highways, embankments, warehouses and light industrial buildings. The subsections cover embankments, bridge approach fills, bridge abutment and foundation support, and liquefaction.
key_points: Functions: bearing, settlement reduction, faster settlement, slope stability, liquefaction mitigation (p. 5-6).
sections.applicability: Matching aggregate column functions to project needs.

sections.title: Embankments
sections.summary: Aggregate columns stabilize large area loads such as highway embankments where conventional embankments fail stability, including moderate-to-high fills on soft soil, MSE-contained fills, slope stabilization and highway widening over soft soil (p. 5-6).
sections.body: A typical application is stabilization of large area loads such as highway embankments, where conventional embankments cannot be built for stability reasons (p. 5-6). Applications include moderate-to-high fills on soft soils, fills contained by mechanically stabilized earth, and construction on slopes where stability cannot otherwise be obtained. Slope stabilization is an important related application; a state DOT reported in 1987 using the dry bottom feed vibro-displacement method to solve a slide problem (Sung and Ramsey 1988). Highway widening adjacent to existing highways on moderate-to-high fills over soft cohesive soils, such as in wetlands, makes differential settlement between existing and new construction an important consideration in addition to stability; support of the new fill on aggregate columns is a viable alternative to conventional construction.
key_points: Used where conventional embankments cannot be built for stability (p. 5-6).
Highway widening over soft soil: differential settlement between old and new fill is a key concern (p. 5-6).
sections.applicability: Embankment and widening projects over soft cohesive soils.

sections.title: Bridge Approach Fills
sections.summary: Aggregate columns support bridge approach fills, improving stability and reducing settlement at the bridge joint; column-supported fills can be built higher and faster, possibly shortening bridges (pp. 5-6 to 5-7).
sections.body: Aggregate columns can support bridge approach fills, provide stability and reduce the costly maintenance problem of settlement at the joint between approach fill and bridge (p. 5-6). The manual cites a state DOT that used 13,000 lineal feet of aggregate columns in 1989 to support MSE walls at an overpass, and 42,000 lineal feet of 13 to 20 foot long columns in 1990 on another project. Column-supported embankments can be built to greater heights than conventional approach embankments over soft soils, so bridge lengths may be reduced by extending the approach fills (p. 5-7). Fills can also be placed faster because of accelerated drainage and consolidation and the increase in shear strength supplied by the columns.
key_points: Reduces settlement at the bridge/approach joint (p. 5-6).
Higher approach fills may shorten bridges; faster fill placement from drainage and strength gain (p. 5-7).
sections.applicability: Approach embankments on soft ground at bridges.

sections.title: Bridge Abutment and Foundation Support
sections.summary: Aggregate columns can support bridge abutments, MSE walls at abutments, and single span bridges with their abutments and approach fills as an alternative to piles, minimizing bridge-to-fill differential settlement (p. 5-7).
sections.body: Aggregate columns can support bridge abutments at sites not capable of supporting abutments on conventional shallow foundations; an important additional application at such sites is MSE walls supported on stone columns (p. 5-7). Another potentially cost effective alternative to pile foundations at unfavorable sites is to support single span bridges, their abutments and their approach fills on aggregate columns, which minimizes differential settlement between the bridge and approach fill.
key_points: Single span bridge, abutments and approach fill all on aggregate columns minimizes differential settlement (p. 5-7).
sections.applicability: Abutment support where shallow foundations alone are inadequate.

sections.title: Liquefaction
sections.summary: In seismic areas aggregate columns reduce the liquefaction potential of cohesionless soils beneath embankments, abutments and shallow foundations and around existing or proposed pile foundations (p. 5-7).
sections.body: In earthquake prone areas aggregate columns can be used to reduce the liquefaction potential of cohesionless soils supporting embankments, abutments and soils beneath shallow foundations (p. 5-7). They can also reduce the liquefaction potential of cohesionless soils surrounding existing or proposed pile foundations, an application used quite extensively for major bridges on pile foundations through liquefiable soils in the Pacific Northwest.
key_points: Mitigates liquefaction under embankments, abutments, shallow foundations and around piles (p. 5-7).
sections.applicability: Liquefaction mitigation in cohesionless soils.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages of Aggregate Columns
sections.summary: Container heading for the advantages and disadvantages of aggregate columns compared with deep foundations, removal and replacement, preloading and high-vibration methods (pp. 5-7 to 5-8).
sections.body: Section 2.2 (p. 5-7) sets out the advantages and the potential disadvantages of aggregate columns in two subsections, covering economy relative to deep foundations and excavation, low vibration, speed, seismic benefits and drainage, against the limits in very soft and organic soils, obstructions, cost, spoil handling and casing.
sections.applicability: Weighing aggregate columns against other foundation and ground modification options.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Aggregate columns can replace deep foundations with shallow foundations, are cheaper than deep removal and replacement, are low-vibration, faster than preloading, reduce seismic settlement and provide drainage (pp. 5-7 to 5-8).
sections.body: Aggregate columns are a technical and potentially economical alternative to deep foundations, improving the soil enough to allow less expensive shallow foundations (p. 5-7). They are more economical than removal and replacement of deep poor bearing soils, particularly on larger sites with shallow groundwater. Where infrastructure precludes high-vibration techniques such as pile driving, dynamic compaction or deep blasting, the low-vibration aggregate column technique is often viable. Installation can be achieved quicker than preloading. In seismic areas aggregate columns can reduce dynamic settlements to acceptable levels and in some cases densify soils beyond the threshold of liquefaction (p. 5-8). With low fines content aggregate they also provide radial drainage and a vertical drainage path for excess pore pressure dissipation, as well as densifying liquefiable soils.
key_points: Alternative to deep foundations; allows shallow foundations (p. 5-7).
Low-vibration; faster than preloading (p. 5-7).
Radial and vertical drainage when low fines aggregate is used (p. 5-8).
sections.applicability: Making the case for aggregate columns over alternatives.

sections.title: Disadvantages
sections.summary: Aggregate columns are unsuitable in peat, organics and very soft clays thicker than a column diameter; obstructions may need predrilling; cost, spoil water, lateral displacement, contaminated spoil and casing are other drawbacks (p. 5-8).
sections.body: Aggregate columns are not a solution for all soft soil problems (p. 5-8). Strata of peat and other organic materials, and very soft clays thicker than the column diameter, can be inappropriate because they offer inadequate lateral support to form the column or ensure long-term performance. Dense overburden, boulders, cobbles or other obstructions may require predrilling for stone columns; rammed aggregate piers, which auger a hole, can generally overcome this. Cost relative to other solutions can be a disadvantage. Channeling and disposing of spoil water in wet feed construction, and lateral ground displacement in the dry process, may be major disadvantages at some locations. Spoil removal from rammed aggregate piers or predrilled stone columns may be a major disadvantage where soils are contaminated. Rammed aggregate piers are more costly when casing is required, and with casing may not densify granular soils as effectively as stone columns.
key_points: Peat, organics and very soft clay thicker than the column diameter can be inappropriate (p. 5-8).
Obstructions may need predrilling for stone columns (p. 5-8).
Casing raises rammed aggregate pier cost and may reduce densification of granular soils (p. 5-8).
sections.applicability: Identifying site conditions that argue against aggregate columns.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Aggregate columns have been successful in improving embankment and slope stability, increasing bearing resistance, reducing total and differential settlement, reducing liquefaction potential and increasing the time rate of settlement (p. 5-8).
sections.body: The aggregate column technique has been successful in (1) improving stability of embankments and natural slopes, (2) increasing bearing resistance, (3) reducing total and differential settlements, (4) reducing liquefaction potential of cohesionless soils and (5) increasing the time rate of settlement (p. 5-8). The feasibility evaluation is discussed under geotechnical, environmental and site considerations.
key_points: Five demonstrated benefits: stability, bearing, settlement, liquefaction, settlement rate (p. 5-8).
sections.applicability: Framework for evaluating aggregate column feasibility.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Geotechnical feasibility: soils with under 15% passing #200 and under 2% clay densify; clayey soils are reinforced; typical limits include 110 kips per column, strengths 300 to 1000 psf, 50-70% settlement reduction, and maximum depths of 100 ft (stone columns) and 35 ft (RAPs) (pp. 5-8 to 5-9).
sections.body: Densification from vibro systems depends on soil type, silt and clay content, plasticity, initial relative density, vibrator type, stone shape and durability, column area, spacing and energy (p. 5-8). Soils with less than 15 percent passing the #200 sieve and clay contents below 2 percent densify from vibration; clayey soils do not, and improvement there is measured by the percent of soil replaced or displaced, i.e. reinforcement. Feasibility factors (p. 5-9): (1) column loading should be fairly uniform and is limited by lateral support; with good support a maximum of 110 kips per column is typical, and the composite factored bearing resistance is increased to 2,000 to 8,000 psf. (2) The most significant improvement is in compressible silts and clays with shear strength 300 to 1000 psf. (3) Do not use in highly sensitive soils; take special care in organics, peat or layers with undrained strength below 300 psf; organic layers thicker than one to two diameters make consistent diameters questionable. (4) Stone columns typically reduce settlement by 50 to 70 percent of the unimproved response and differential settlement to 5 to 15 percent; rammed aggregate piers can reduce settlement to under 1 inch in some conditions. (5) A practical upper limit for stone columns is an undrained strength of 1000 to 2000 psf; stiffer soils are commonly pre-bored at added cost. (6) Rammed aggregate piers in soils that do not stand open may need temporary casing. (7) Maximum practical depths are 100 feet for stone columns and 35 feet for rammed aggregate piers.
key_points: Vibro densification works with <15% passing #200 and <2% clay (p. 5-8).
Typical maximum 110 kips per column; composite factored bearing 2,000-8,000 psf (p. 5-9).
Best improvement in silts and clays with su 300 to 1000 psf (p. 5-9).
Care where su < 300 psf, organics or peat; not for highly sensitive soils (p. 5-9).
Stone columns reduce settlement 50-70%; differential to 5-15% of unimproved (p. 5-9).
Stone column penetration limit su 1000 to 2000 psf; pre-bore beyond (p. 5-9).
Maximum practical depth: 100 ft stone columns, 35 ft rammed aggregate piers (p. 5-9).
sections.applicability: Geotechnical screening of soils and loads for stone columns and rammed aggregate piers.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Installation method selection should consider environmental effects; soil spoils, particularly fines from air or water jetting, must be contained, and an alternate column system that does not replace in situ soil may be chosen (pp. 5-9 to 5-10).
sections.body: Selection of the aggregate column installation method should consider the environmental effects of installation (p. 5-9). Soil spoils must be contained, particularly fines from air or water jetting operations (p. 5-10). The designer may select an alternate column system that does not replace the in situ soils.
key_points: Contain spoils, especially fines from jetting (p. 5-10).
sections.applicability: Environmental review of aggregate column installation methods.

sections.title: Site Consideration
sections.summary: Aggregate column equipment needs headroom typically 8 to 10 ft more than the column penetration depth; adjacent structures must be monitored for heave with vibro-displacement stone columns (p. 5-10).
sections.body: Site conditions should always be considered when selecting a ground modification technology (p. 5-10). Installation of aggregate columns requires sufficient headroom for the construction equipment, typically 8 to 10 feet more than the depth of penetration of the column. Adjacent buildings and structures must be monitored for heave when vibro-displacement stone columns are used.
key_points: Headroom typically 8 to 10 ft more than column depth (p. 5-10).
Monitor adjacent structures for heave with vibro-displacement (p. 5-10).
sections.applicability: Site logistics for aggregate column equipment.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: The major limitation is that aggregate columns are not appropriate in very soft, sensitive fine-grained soils and organics; stone may not be locally available, and rammed aggregate piers are limited in depth to typically 35 ft (p. 5-10).
sections.body: The major limitation of aggregate columns is that they are not appropriate in very soft and sensitive fine-grained soils and organics (p. 5-10). Stone may not be readily available near the project site, with potentially significant cost ramifications. Rammed aggregate piers have the additional limitation of column depth, typically 35 feet.
key_points: Not appropriate in very soft, sensitive fine-grained soils and organics (p. 5-10).
Rammed aggregate pier depth typically limited to 35 ft (p. 5-10).
sections.applicability: Recognizing when aggregate columns should not be used.

sections.title: Alternative Modification Methods
sections.summary: Alternatives similar in concept to aggregate piers include gravel drains, sand compaction piles and rammed stone columns; other alternatives (PVDs, deep and mass mixing, jet grout) are in Chapters 2, 7 and 8 (pp. 5-10 to 5-11).
sections.body: Alternative methods similar in concept to aggregate piers have been used: gravel drains, sand compaction piles and rammed stone columns (p. 5-10). Other alternatives are covered elsewhere in the manual (p. 5-11): prefabricated vertical drains with or without preloading (Chapter 2), deep and mass mixing methods (Chapter 7) and jetted grout columns (Chapter 8).
key_points: PVDs - Chapter 2; deep and mass mixing - Chapter 7; jet grouting - Chapter 8 (p. 5-11).
sections.applicability: Listing alternatives to compare with aggregate columns.

sections.title: Gravel Drains
sections.summary: Gravel drains, used in Japan, are built by backfilling inside a casing and densifying the stone with an interior vibrator; they drain well but do little to densify surrounding soil, and may not prevent liquefaction alone (p. 5-10).
sections.body: In Japan gravel drains are installed by backfilling inside a casing and densifying the stone with an interior vibrator as the casing is extracted (p. 5-10). This provides a good drain but does little to densify the soil outside the casing. For soils with high liquefaction potential, gravel drains alone may not handle the excess pore pressures and liquefaction may still occur.
key_points: Good drainage but little densification outside the casing (p. 5-10).
sections.applicability: Considering drainage-only columns for liquefaction.

sections.title: Sand Compaction Piles
sections.summary: Sand compaction piles are built by driving a steel casing with a vibratory hammer and filling it with sand as it is extracted; see Kitazume (2005) (p. 5-10).
sections.body: Sand compaction piles are also used extensively in Japan (p. 5-10). They are constructed by using a vibratory hammer to install a steel casing to the desired elevation; the casing is filled with sand as it is extracted. More information is in The Sand Compaction Pile Method (Kitazume 2005).
key_points: Reference: Kitazume (2005) (p. 5-10).
sections.applicability: Background on a sand-column alternative.

sections.title: Rammed Stone Columns
sections.summary: Rammed stone columns are built by driving a casing, placing granular backfill and dropping a heavy weight on it as the casing is withdrawn; slow (250 ft/shift/rig) and not economically competitive (pp. 5-10 to 5-11).
sections.body: In Belgium rammed stone columns have been constructed by driving a casing, placing granular backfill and dropping a heavy weight on the stone as the casing is extracted (p. 5-10). While some compaction of the surrounding soil can be achieved, it is a very slow process, about 250 ft per shift per rig, and therefore not economically competitive (p. 5-11).
key_points: Production about 250 ft/shift/rig; not economically competitive (p. 5-11).
sections.applicability: Background on a slow casing-and-drop-weight alternative.

sections.title: Construction Materials and Equipment
sections.summary: Container heading for construction methods, equipment and backfill materials for stone columns (Section 3.1) and rammed aggregate columns (Section 3.2) (p. 5-12).
sections.body: Section 3.0 (p. 5-12) describes construction materials and equipment, first for stone columns (vibro-replacement and vibro-displacement construction, equipment and backfill) and then for rammed aggregate columns (the replacement method and backfill).
sections.applicability: Construction methods and materials for aggregate columns.

sections.title: Stone Columns
sections.summary: Container for stone column construction: the vibro-replacement (wet, top feed) and vibro-displacement (dry, top or bottom feed) methods, the vibrator and rig equipment, and backfill gradation (pp. 5-12 to 5-23).
sections.body: Section 3.1 covers stone columns: construction by vibro-replacement and vibro-displacement with the equipment used (Section 3.1.1) and the backfill material (Section 3.1.2) (pp. 5-12 to 5-23).
sections.applicability: Stone column construction.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Stone columns are built by vibro-replacement (wet, top feed) or vibro-displacement (dry, top or bottom feed); the dry process is typically required where environmental concerns are strong, the wet process is more economical otherwise (p. 5-12).
sections.body: The primary methods of constructing stone columns are vibro-replacement (wet, top feed) and vibro-displacement (dry, top or bottom feed) (p. 5-12). Where environmental concerns are strong, the dry process will typically be required; the wet process is more economical when environmental concerns are less relevant. The processes are illustrated in Figure 5-2 (top feed vibro-replacement) and Figure 5-3 (bottom feed vibro-displacement).
key_points: Dry process where environmental concerns are strong; wet process more economical otherwise (p. 5-12).
figures: Figure 5-2: Top feed vibro-replacement.
Figure 5-3: Bottom feed vibro-displacement.
sections.applicability: Choosing the stone column installation process.

sections.title: Vibro-Replacement (Wet, Top Feed)
sections.summary: The wet process jets water to open a hole, retracts the probe in increments and adds stone from the surface, re-penetrating each increment; best for soft to firm soils with su of 300 to 1000 psf and a high groundwater table (p. 5-13).
sections.body: The original stone column technique, vibro-replacement or the wet process, uses a high-pressure jet of water to open a hole that the probe follows into the ground (p. 5-13). The probe is then retracted in increments and stone is introduced into the void from the surface (Figure 5-2). After each increment the probe is lowered into the new column material, densifying and compacting the stone column and, depending on fines content, potentially the surrounding soil. The method is best suited for sites with soft to firm soils with undrained shear strengths of 300 to 1000 psf and a high groundwater table.
key_points: Best for su 300 to 1000 psf and high groundwater (p. 5-13).
sections.applicability: Wet top feed stone column installation.

sections.title: Vibro-Displacement (Dry, Top and Bottom Feed)
sections.summary: Dry top and bottom feed techniques avoid jetting water effluent; the vibrator enters by oscillation, deadweight, air jetting and/or pre-augering; stone is fed from the surface for short columns or through a tremie tube to the tip for deeper or unstable holes (p. 5-13).
sections.body: Because effluent from vibro-replacement contains the finer in situ soil, its containment, removal and disposal caused environmental problems, and dry top and bottom feed techniques were developed (p. 5-13). The vibrator is inserted without jetting water, using its oscillations and deadweight, air jetting and/or pre-augering. For shorter columns stone can still be fed from the surface into the annulus around the vibrator (Figure 5-2). For deeper treatment or where the hole may collapse, the stone is fed to the bottom of the vibrator through an attached tremie tube (Figure 5-3). The first major US use of the dry bottom feed system was a dam foundation in 1985 (Dobson 1987).
key_points: No jetting water; uses vibration, deadweight, air jetting or pre-augering (p. 5-13).
Bottom feed through a tremie tube for deep or collapsing holes (p. 5-13).
sections.applicability: Dry stone column installation where effluent is not acceptable.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: Stone column equipment: vibrator on extension tubes with air or water jetting, crane or base machine, stone delivery system and control devices; vibrators 12-16 in. diameter, 10-16 ft long, 22-125 kW, up to 60 kips at 1200-3000 rpm; continuous construction records (pp. 5-13 to 5-22).
sections.body: Equipment comprises a vibrator suspended from extension tubes with air or water jetting, a crane or base machine, a stone delivery system and control and verification devices (p. 5-13). The vibrator ranges from 12 to 16 inches in diameter and about 10 to 16 feet long (Figures 5-4, 5-5). Horizontal vibrations near its base come from eccentric weights driven by an electric or hydraulic motor; early motors were 22 to 60 kW, recent ones up to 125 kW, with centrifugal forces up to 60 kips at 1200 to 3000 rpm (p. 5-15). Wear plates, fins, extension tubes and an elastic coupling isolating vibration from the crane are described. Water or air is fed to the vibrator nose to aid penetration; a 33-foot probe can be handled by a 40 ton crane with a 40-foot boom. Stone is handled by front end loaders; top feed end-dumps it into the hole, bottom feed uses a skip (or a 6-inch hose) feeding pipes to the vibrator nose (Figures 5-6 to 5-9). A marine double-lock gravel pump delivers stone to the vibrator tip underwater using air pressure (p. 5-19, Figure 5-10). Instrumentation recording depth, power consumption and stone consumption against time, used in the US since 1993, gives printouts for each column (p. 5-20, Figures 5-11, 5-12).
key_points: Vibrator 12-16 in. diameter, about 10-16 ft long (p. 5-13).
Motors 22-60 kW early, up to 125 kW now; up to 60 kips at 1200-3000 rpm (p. 5-15).
A 33-ft probe can be handled by a 40 ton crane with a 40-ft boom (p. 5-15).
Construction instrumentation records depth, power and stone consumption (p. 5-20).

sections.title: Backfill Material
sections.summary: Stone column backfill depends on technique, subsoil, application and availability; vibro-replacement uses subangular or angular gravel of nearly uniform 1.0- to 2.5-inch grading; vibro-displacement uses well graded 0.4- to 3-inch (or 4-inch) stone; bottom feed is limited to 0.4 to 1.4 inch (p. 5-23).
sections.body: Size, gradation and shape of stone column backfill depend on the construction technique, the subsoil properties, the application and local availability of materials (p. 5-23). Drainage characteristics are crucial for liquefaction prevention and shear strength for slope stabilization, while neither is generally critical for increasing bearing resistance. For vibro-replacement, subangular or angular gravel of nearly uniform grading 1.0 to 2.5 inches is often used; it passes easily around the vibrating probe, and larger in situ material suspended in the water fills voids, giving a rigid column. Keeping flushing water flowing at all times washes out infiltrating fines and stabilizes the hole, and keeping the probe in the hole improves stability. For vibro-displacement, well graded backfill from 0.4 to 3 inches, or up to 4 inches, is generally used for interlock and void filling, the finer sizes giving an intermediate size between clay and gravel. The bottom feed method is restricted to about 0.4 to 1.4 inch aggregate to avoid blocking the equipment.
key_points: Vibro-replacement: nearly uniform 1.0 to 2.5 in. subangular or angular gravel (p. 5-23).
Vibro-displacement: well graded 0.4 to 3 in. (up to 4 in.) (p. 5-23).
Bottom feed: about 0.4 to 1.4 in. to avoid blockage (p. 5-23).

sections.title: Rammed Aggregate Columns
sections.summary: Container for rammed aggregate pier construction: the replacement method of drilling, placing and ramming lifts, the drill, tamper and loader equipment, and the backfill aggregate used (pp. 5-23 to 5-26).
sections.body: Section 3.2 covers rammed aggregate columns: construction by the replacement method with its equipment (Section 3.2.1) and the backfill material (Section 3.2.2) (pp. 5-23 to 5-26).
sections.applicability: Rammed aggregate pier construction.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Rammed aggregate piers are built by the replacement method: excavate (cased if needed), place a 24-inch open graded stone lift and ram it to form a bulb, then ram 12-inch lifts; equipment is an excavator drill, an excavator tamper delivering 245 to 650 kip-lbf per foot per lift, and a skid-steer loader (pp. 5-23 to 5-26).
sections.body: The primary method for rammed aggregate piers is the replacement method (p. 5-23, Figure 5-13): excavate the pier to design depth, using casing if the hole will not stay open; place open graded stone at the bottom in a 24-inch thick lift; ram it; then place and ram 12-inch lifts until the top of column elevation is reached (p. 5-24). Equipment (Figures 5-14, 5-15; p. 5-26) consists of an excavator-mounted drill with typically 2- to 3-foot diameter tools, an excavator-mounted tamper (a modified concrete breaker with a composite alloy shaft and beveled hammer) capable of delivering 245 to 650 kip-lbf per 1 foot per lift of tamping energy, which densifies the aggregate and forces it laterally into the sidewalls, and a skid-steer loader, usually track-driven, delivering aggregate. The tamper should be at least 85% of the plan area of the cavity.
key_points: Bottom lift 24 in. of open graded stone; subsequent lifts 12 in. (p. 5-24).
Tamping energy 245 to 650 kip-lbf per 1 ft per lift (p. 5-26).
Tamper at least 85% of the cavity plan area (p. 5-26).

sections.title: Backfill Material
sections.summary: Clean 1- to 3-inch stone is commonly specified for the rammed aggregate pier bottom bulb; the same is used throughout if radial drainage is part of the design, otherwise a well-graded base course aggregate (p. 5-26).
sections.body: For rammed aggregate pier construction, clean 1- to 3-inch stone is commonly specified for the bottom bulb (p. 5-26). The same material is used throughout the pier if radial drainage of the pier is included in the design solution; otherwise a well-graded base course aggregate is used.
key_points: Bottom bulb: clean 1 to 3 in. stone (p. 5-26).
Well-graded base course aggregate unless radial drainage is required (p. 5-26).
sections.applicability: Specifying rammed aggregate pier aggregate.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Container heading for design of stone columns (Section 4.1), rammed aggregate piers (4.2), worked design examples (4.3) and design verification by load and in situ testing (4.4) (p. 5-27).
sections.body: Section 4.0 (p. 5-27) presents the design of aggregate columns: stone columns with the unit cell, area replacement ratio, stress ratio, capacity, settlement, rate of settlement, shear strength and seismic design; rammed aggregate piers with the two-layer settlement approach; two design examples; and design verification.
sections.applicability: Design of stone columns and rammed aggregate piers.

sections.title: Stone Columns
sections.summary: Container for stone column design: design considerations, the procedure (unit cell, area replacement ratio, stress ratio, capacity, settlement, rate, shear strength) and seismic design (pp. 5-27 to 5-42).
sections.body: Section 4.1 covers stone column design: design considerations (4.1.1), the design procedure with the unit cell, area replacement ratio, spacing and diameter, stress ratio, vertical capacity, settlement, rate of settlement and shear strength increase (4.1.2), and seismic design (4.1.3) (pp. 5-27 to 5-42).
sections.applicability: Stone column design.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Stone column design is largely semi-empirical and similar for wet and dry methods; soil-column composites stiffen with closer spacing, larger area and higher stone friction angle; columns need lateral support against bulging, should end in a denser stratum, and attract load as the soil consolidates (pp. 5-27 to 5-28).
sections.body: Although backfill placement and gradation differ between vibro-replacement and vibro-displacement, the design approach is similar (p. 5-27). Design theory development is outside the scope; FHWA (1983) gives in-depth criteria, Priebe (1995) updated earlier work and was widely used, and GeoTechTools gives the most current guidance. Design is to a large extent semi-empirical; recommendations are given for bearing, settlement and stability and should be supplemented by experience and judgment. Methods range from semi-empirical to finite element, indexed to full-scale tests and models. Weak soils reinforced with stone columns act as a composite with stiffness increasing with reduced spacing, larger column area and stone friction angle. The columns are stiffer than the soil and rely on its lateral support, so they must have adequate lateral support to preclude bulging failure and typically terminate in a denser stratum to preclude bearing failure. Because the column settles less, it carries by arching a larger part of the load, and further consolidation transfers more load to it until equilibrium, decreasing settlement of the whole foundation (p. 5-28).
key_points: Stone column design is largely semi-empirical (p. 5-27).
Columns need lateral support to prevent bulging and should end in a denser stratum (p. 5-27).
Load transfers to the stiffer column by arching as the soil consolidates (pp. 5-27 to 5-28).
sections.applicability: Understanding the mechanics behind stone column design.

sections.title: Design Procedure
sections.summary: Seven-step embankment design process for stone columns: unimproved settlement and stability, assume area replacement ratio and diameter, find spacing, check column capacity, compute settlement, check time rate, check global stability (p. 5-28).
sections.body: Stone columns are selected to increase bearing resistance, reduce settlement, accelerate consolidation, increase shear strength, reduce liquefaction potential, or a combination (p. 5-28). Preliminary design methods are outlined. The generalized process for embankment support is: (1) design the embankment without stone columns to find overall settlement and global stability and whether ground modification is required; (2) assume an area replacement ratio and column diameter; (3) determine the spacing from them; (4) check the load bearing resistance of the column and revise the diameter if needed; (5) determine the total settlement of the embankment on stone columns; (6) check the time rate of settlement and consider changing spacing if too slow; (7) check global stability.
key_points: Start from area replacement ratio and diameter, then spacing (p. 5-28).
Check capacity, settlement, time rate and global stability in turn (p. 5-28).
sections.applicability: Preliminary design sequence for stone column supported embankments.

sections.title: Unit Cell Concept
sections.summary: For settlement and stability analysis the tributary soil around each column (a hexagon in a triangular pattern) is idealized as an equivalent circle of diameter De, the unit cell, with the column at its center (pp. 5-28 to 5-30).
sections.body: For settlement and stability analyses it is convenient to associate the tributary area of soil surrounding each stone column with that column (p. 5-28; Figures 5-16 and 5-17). Although the tributary area forms a regular hexagon about the column, it can be closely approximated by an equivalent circle of the same total area (p. 5-30). The resulting equivalent cylinder of diameter De, enclosing the tributary soil and one stone column, is known as the unit cell; the stone column is concentric with its exterior boundary.
key_points: Unit cell: equivalent cylinder of diameter De with the same area as the tributary hexagon (p. 5-30).
The column is concentric with the unit cell (p. 5-30).
figures: Figure 5-16: Equilateral triangular pattern of stone columns.
Figure 5-17: Unit cell idealization.
sections.applicability: Idealizing a column grid for settlement and stability calculations.

sections.title: Area Replacement Ratio
sections.summary: The area replacement ratio alpha_sc = A_sc / A (Eq. 5-1) is the fraction of the unit cell area replaced by compacted stone; typical values are 0.10 to 0.30; the area improvement ratio a_sc is its inverse (pp. 5-30 to 5-31).
sections.body: The volume of soil replaced by stone columns has an important effect on performance (p. 5-30). The area replacement ratio, alpha_sc, is defined as the fraction of soil tributary to the stone column replaced by stone (p. 5-31): alpha_sc = A_sc / A (Eq. 5-1), where A_sc is the area of the stone column after compaction and A is the total area within the unit cell. Typical ratios used are in the range 0.10 to 0.30. The literature also describes the ratio a_sc, the area improvement ratio, which is the inverse of the area replacement ratio.
key_points: alpha_sc = A_sc / A (Eq. 5-1, p. 5-31).
A_sc is the column area after compaction; A is the unit cell area (p. 5-31).
Typical alpha_sc 0.10 to 0.30 (p. 5-31).
Area improvement ratio is the inverse of alpha_sc (p. 5-31).
equations: Eq. 5-1: alpha_sc = A_sc / A; area replacement ratio (A_sc = area of stone column after compaction, A = total area within the unit cell)
sections.applicability: Quantifying how much soil a stone column grid replaces.

sections.title: Spacing and Diameter
sections.summary: Stone column diameters vary from 1.5 to 4 ft, typically 3.0 to 3.6 ft for the dry method and larger for wet; triangular, square or rectangular grids at 5 to 12 ft center-to-center, extending beyond the loaded area (p. 5-31).
sections.body: Stone column diameters vary between 1.5 and 4 feet but are typically 3.0 to 3.6 feet for the dry method and somewhat larger for the wet method (p. 5-31). Triangular, square or rectangular grid patterns are used, generally with center-to-center spacing of 5 to 12 feet. For footing support the columns are installed in rows or clusters. For both footing and wide area support they should extend beyond the loaded area.
key_points: Diameter 1.5 to 4 ft; typically 3.0 to 3.6 ft (dry), larger (wet) (p. 5-31).
Spacing generally 5 to 12 ft center-to-center (p. 5-31).
Extend columns beyond the loaded area (p. 5-31).
sections.applicability: Preliminary selection of stone column diameter and grid.

sections.title: Stress Ratio
sections.summary: Stress concentration (stress ratio) n = sigma_sc / sigma_soil (Eq. 5-2) under equal strain; measured 2.0 to 5.0; 2.5 often used for preliminary design; equilibrium q = sigma_sc alpha_sc + sigma_soil (1 - alpha_sc) (Eq. 5-3) gives the soil and column stresses (Eqs. 5-4, 5-5) (pp. 5-31 to 5-32).
sections.body: The relative stiffness of column and soil, and the column diameter and spacing, determine how the applied vertical load is shared (p. 5-31). Because deflections are approximately equal (the equal strain assumption, supported by field measurements and finite element analyses), the stiffer column carries a greater stress. The stress concentration or stress ratio n, the stress in the stone column divided by the in situ soil stress, depends on relative stiffness, column length, area ratio and the granular blanket over the columns. Measured values are generally 2.0 to 5.0, and theory indicates n increases with time, since secondary settlement of the cohesive soil exceeds that of the column. Selecting the design stress ratio is the key element of preliminary design and is largely experience based (p. 5-32). A high ratio (3 to 4) may be warranted for very weak soil and very tight spacing; for stronger soils and large spacings lower bound ratios (2 to 2.5) apply; 2.5 is often conservatively used for stability and bearing calculations. With n and alpha_sc, the column stress sigma_sc and soil stress sigma_soil for an average unit-cell stress q follow from Eqs. 5-2 to 5-5.
key_points: n = sigma_sc / sigma_soil (Eq. 5-2, p. 5-32).
Measured n generally 2.0 to 5.0; increases with time (p. 5-31).
n of 3 to 4 for very weak soil and tight spacing; 2 to 2.5 for stronger soil and wide spacing (p. 5-32).
n = 2.5 is often conservatively used for preliminary stability and bearing (p. 5-32).
equations: Eq. 5-2: n = sigma_sc / sigma_soil; stress concentration (stress ratio), column stress over soil stress
Eq. 5-3: q = sigma_sc (alpha_sc) + sigma_soil (1 - alpha_sc); equilibrium of vertical forces over the unit cell
Eq. 5-4: sigma_soil = q / [1 + (n - 1) alpha_sc]; stress on the unimproved soil
Eq. 5-5: sigma_sc = n q / [1 + (n - 1) alpha_sc]; stress on the stone column
sections.applicability: Splitting the applied load between stone columns and soil.

sections.title: Stone Column Vertical Load Capacity
sections.summary: Failure modes of single columns and groups (Figures 5-18 to 5-20); avoid bulging in weak or organic layers; nominal bearing resistance q_n = c N_c (Eq. 5-6) with N_c 18 to 22 (22 for stiffer, 18 for low stiffness soils), a resistance factor of 3, and typical single column design loads of 40 to 60 kips (pp. 5-32 to 5-35).
sections.body: Possible failure modes of single stone columns and groups are illustrated in Figures 5-18 to 5-20 (p. 5-32). Local bulging failures in very weak or organic layers of limited thickness (Figure 5-19) should be avoided; bulging affects settlement magnitude and rate, stability and column strength (p. 5-35). A bulging analysis of a single column used for group behavior gives an approximate conservative solution. Rational prediction of group bearing under rigid or flexible loads is still developing, so experience and judgment should accompany theory. Group capacity is frequently taken as the single column capacity times the number of columns, which model studies indicate is slightly conservative for soft cohesive soils. The nominal bearing resistance of an isolated or group column is q_n = c N_c (Eq. 5-6), where c is the undrained shear strength of the surrounding cohesive soil and N_c the bearing capacity factor; values 18 to 22 give good estimates. Cavity expansion theory makes N_c depend on soil compressibility: N_c = 22 for soils with reasonably high initial stiffness (inorganic soft-to-stiff clays and silts) and 18 for low stiffness soils (peats, organic cohesive soils, very soft clays with PI > 30), based on back-analysis of field tests. A resistance factor of 3 is recommended with Eq. 5-6. Typical single column design loads are 40 to 60 kips in soft to medium stiff clays.
key_points: N_c = 22 for stiffer inorganic soils; 18 for peats, organic soils and very soft clays with PI > 30 (p. 5-35).
Resistance factor of 3 recommended with Eq. 5-6 (p. 5-35).
Typical single column design loads 40 to 60 kips (p. 5-35).
Group capacity = single capacity x number of columns is slightly conservative in soft clay (p. 5-35).
equations: Eq. 5-6: q_n = c N_c; nominal bearing resistance of a stone column (c = undrained shear strength of surrounding cohesive soil, N_c = bearing capacity factor, 18 to 22)

Figure 5-19: Failure modes of a single stone column in a non-homogeneous cohesive soil.
Figure 5-20: Failure modes of stone column groups.
