sections.title: Settlement
sections.summary: Settlement reduction is expressed as the settlement ratio n (settlement without columns over settlement with columns) versus the area replacement or improvement ratio; Figure 5-21 compares theories and field data; the Priebe curve gives an upper bound and the FHWA (1983) Equilibrium Method, about equal to Balaam, an average or lower bound (pp. 5-36 to 5-37).
sections.body: Settlement reduction has been estimated by pseudo-elastic and elasto-plastic methods for isolated and widespread loading using the unit cell concept (p. 5-36). The predicted improvement is often expressed as the settlement ratio n, the ratio of settlement without stone columns to that with stone columns, related to the area replacement ratio (alpha_sc) or the area improvement ratio (1/alpha_sc). Settlement of the non-improved zone is found by conventional analyses. Theoretical predictions and field measurements are compared in Figure 5-21 (Greenwood and Kirsch 1984). Han (2015) presents three methods for granular column reinforced foundations: the stress reduction method, the improvement factor method and the elastic-plastic method. In Figure 5-21 the settlement ratio was found analytically as a function of E_sc/E_soil or of column strength relative to the soil shear strength c_u (p. 5-37). For preliminary estimates the Priebe curve may be used to evaluate the upper bound effectiveness and cost at various spacings. The Equilibrium Method of FHWA (1983) is roughly equivalent to the Balaam relationships in Figure 5-21 and represents an average or lower bound estimate suitable for preliminary analyses. The chapter prints no closed-form settlement improvement equation; the Priebe curve is read from the figure (applied in Section 4.3.2.3 with Figure 5-27).
key_points: Settlement ratio n = settlement without columns / settlement with columns (p. 5-36).
Plotted against the area improvement ratio A/A_sc = 1/alpha_sc in Figure 5-21 (p. 5-36).
Priebe curve: upper bound effectiveness for preliminary estimates (p. 5-37).
FHWA (1983) Equilibrium Method ~ Balaam: average or lower bound (p. 5-37).
Han (2015): stress reduction, improvement factor and elastic-plastic methods (p. 5-36).
figures: Figure 5-21: Comparison of elastic theories and field observations.
sections.applicability: Preliminary estimate of settlement reduction from stone columns.

sections.title: Rate of Settlement
sections.summary: Stone columns accelerate settlement by radial drainage, computed as for sand drains and PVDs (Chapter 2); smear is roughly modeled by reducing the column diameter by 50 to 80 percent of design diameter, with more smear for dry-displacement and sensitive clays (p. 5-37).
sections.body: Stone columns substantially alter the time rate of settlement because radial drainage governs (p. 5-37). Time-rate computations are therefore identical to those for vertical sand drains and prefabricated vertical drains (Chapter 2). The effect of disturbance or smear during installation, which reduces radial flow, can be roughly accounted for by reducing the column diameter by 50 to 80 percent of its design diameter. A larger disturbance or smear zone should be anticipated with the dry-displacement method and for all installations in sensitive clays.
key_points: Compute as for PVDs and sand drains (Chapter 2) (p. 5-37).
Smear: reduce column diameter by 50 to 80 percent of design diameter (p. 5-37).
sections.applicability: Time rate of consolidation for stone column reinforced clay.

sections.title: Shear Strength Increase
sections.summary: Average composite strength tau = (1 - alpha_sc) c_u + alpha_sc sigma_v tan phi_sc (Eq. 5-7) and unit weight (Eq. 5-8) for stability; may overestimate FS by 10% undrained; phi_sc 40 to 45 degrees; target FS 1.2 to 1.3; discrete column modeling now preferred (pp. 5-37 to 5-39).
sections.body: For slope stability an average shear strength of the soil/stone column composite has been used to estimate embankment stability (p. 5-37, Figure 5-22). Recent research shows the average strength approach may overestimate the factor of safety by 10% for an undrained condition (Zhang et al. 2014; Abusharar and Han 2011) (p. 5-38). The composite strength depends on the soil undrained strength, the column friction, the area replacement ratio, the stress ratio and the loading; close spacing and substantial overburden are needed to mobilize column friction. The average strength and unit weight are given by Eqs. 5-7 and 5-8, where tau is the average weighted shear strength, c_u the undrained strength of the in situ soil, gamma_soil and gamma_sc the unit weights of soil and column, phi_sc the column friction angle, sigma_v the stress due to embankment loading and alpha_sc the area replacement ratio (p. 5-39). The design friction angle of the stone typically varies from 40 to 45 degrees, lower for gravel mixtures and higher for angular crushed stone. In landslide remediation the stress ratio is 1 and the parameters are essentially a weighted average. Analyses may use total stress (phi = 0, end of construction) or effective stress (c = 0, long term); a target factor of safety of 1.2 to 1.3 is considered adequate. Slope stability programs can now model discrete stone columns instead of the average strength method (see GeoTechTools).
key_points: tau = (1 - alpha_sc) c_u + alpha_sc sigma_v tan phi_sc (Eq. 5-7, p. 5-38).
Average strength may overestimate FS by 10% undrained (p. 5-38).
phi_sc typically 40 to 45 degrees (p. 5-39).
Landslide remediation: stress ratio of 1 (p. 5-39).
Target factor of safety 1.2 to 1.3 (p. 5-39).
equations: Eq. 5-7: tau = (1 - alpha_sc) c_u + alpha_sc sigma_v tan phi_sc; average weighted shear strength of the soil/stone column composite
Eq. 5-8: gamma_bar = gamma_sc alpha_sc + gamma_soil (1 - alpha_sc); average unit weight of the composite
figures: Figure 5-22: Notation used in average stress method stability analysis.
sections.applicability: Composite strength parameters for stability analysis of column-supported embankments.

sections.title: Seismic Design
sections.summary: Stone columns mitigate liquefaction by densifying soil, aiding drainage and carrying more seismic stress; the simplified procedure presented considers only densification and suits preliminary design (pp. 5-39 to 5-40).
sections.body: Efforts in the United States have aimed at evaluating liquefaction potential from in situ density data and improving these soils (p. 5-39). Baez and Martin (1992), Hryciw (1995), Baez (1993) and Woeste et al. (2016) give recommendations on quantifying the benefits of stone columns and evaluating the safety factor against liquefaction. The benefits are densification of the soil around the column, facilitated drainage of excess pore water, and the stiffer column accepting higher seismic stress than the soil (p. 5-40). The simplified procedure presented considers only the benefit of soil densification; it is appropriate for preliminary designs and more rigorous analysis may be warranted for final design.
key_points: Three benefits: densification, drainage, stiffer column carries more seismic stress (p. 5-40).
Simplified procedure counts densification only; preliminary design (p. 5-40).
sections.applicability: Preliminary liquefaction mitigation design with stone columns.

sections.title: Soil Density
sections.summary: Liquefaction potential falls with density; cyclic stress ratio CSR_EQ = 0.65 (a_max/g) r_d (sigma_v/sigma_v') (Eq. 5-9) with depth-based r_d expressions; Figure 5-23 (Seed et al. 1985) relates CSR causing liquefaction to (N1)60 for M7.5 to set the required densification (pp. 5-40 to 5-41).
sections.body: Under cyclic loading pore pressure builds more slowly in dense than in loose sand, so liquefaction potential is reduced by increasing density (p. 5-40). Loose sands can deform greatly after initial liquefaction, while dense sands dilate at large strain and keep residual stiffness and strength. Seed et al. (1985) correlated cyclic stress ratio with corrected penetration resistance. The cyclic stress ratio is CSR_EQ = 0.65 (a_max/g) r_d (sigma_v/sigma_v') (Eq. 5-9), with a_max the maximum ground acceleration, sigma_v and sigma_v' the total and effective vertical stress at depth z, and r_d the stress reduction factor. For preliminary design (equations developed for metric units, as printed): r_d = 1.0 - 0.00765z for z <= 30 ft; r_d = 1.174 - 0.0267z for 30 ft < z <= 75 ft (p. 5-41); r_d = 0.744 - 0.008z for 75 ft < z <= 100 ft; r_d = 0.5 for z < 100 ft (as printed). Figure 5-23 relates the stress ratio causing liquefaction to (N1)60 for silty sands in a magnitude 7.5 earthquake and is used to estimate the required improvement in density.
key_points: CSR_EQ = 0.65 (a_max/g) r_d (sigma_v/sigma_v') (Eq. 5-9, p. 5-40).
The manual notes the r_d equations were developed for metric units (p. 5-40).
equations: Eq. 5-9: CSR_EQ = 0.65 (a_max / g) r_d (sigma_v / sigma_v'); cyclic stress ratio induced by the earthquake
figures: Figure 5-23: Relationship between stress ratio causing liquefaction and (N1)60 values for silty sands for 7.5 magnitude earthquakes.
sections.applicability: Required densification target for liquefaction mitigation.

sections.title: Spacing
sections.summary: Stone column spacing for liquefaction: find the required corrected SPT N from Figure 5-23, convert to relative density with Table 4-8, then use Figure 4-34 (Chapter 4) for spacing to reach that resistance midway between columns (p. 5-42).
sections.body: The spacing of stone columns for liquefaction mitigation may be determined by using Figure 5-23 to find the required corrected SPT N value, Table 4-8 of Chapter 4 (Deep Compaction) to correlate SPT N to relative density, and then Figure 4-34 of Chapter 4 to estimate the stone column spacing needed to improve the soil to the required penetration resistance at the mid-point between columns (p. 5-42).
key_points: Figure 5-23 -> Table 4-8 -> Figure 4-34 (Chapter 4) (p. 5-42).
Target is the penetration resistance at the mid-point between columns (p. 5-42).
sections.applicability: Selecting stone column spacing for densification.

sections.title: Permeability
sections.summary: To avoid significant pore pressure generation in the column, its permeability should be at least two orders of magnitude larger than the treated soil, achieved by gradation selection with due regard to piping (p. 5-42).
sections.body: To avoid significant generation of pore water pressure within the stone column, its permeability should be at least two orders of magnitude larger than that of the treated soil (p. 5-42). This can be achieved by selecting the gradation of the stone column, with due regard to the piping considerations that follow.
key_points: Column permeability at least 100 times the treated soil (p. 5-42).
sections.applicability: Gradation selection for draining stone columns.

sections.title: Piping Prevention
sections.summary: Hydraulic gradients may exceed critical during shaking and move fines into the column; the recommended filter criterion is 20 D_S15 < D_G15 < 9 D_S85 (Eq. 5-10) (p. 5-42).
sections.body: Hydraulic gradients may exceed critical gradients (greater than one) and move fines from the natural soil into the open pore structure of the stone column during seismic loading, creating cavities and undesirable volume change, although the short duration of strong motion makes much movement unlikely (p. 5-42). Based on experimental data, the following relationship is recommended for piping prevention under any loading condition: 20 D_S15 < D_G15 < 9 D_S85 (Eq. 5-10), where D_S15 is the soil particle diameter passing 15 percent, D_G15 the gravel (stone) diameter passing 15 percent, and D_S85 the soil diameter passing 85 percent. Adherence ensures maximum permeability and prevents piping of the soil.
equations: Eq. 5-10: 20 D_S15 < D_G15 < 9 D_S85; piping prevention (filter) criterion for stone column gradation
sections.applicability: Checking stone column gradation against the surrounding soil.

sections.title: Rammed Aggregate Piers
sections.summary: Container for rammed aggregate pier design: stress and replacement ratios, the seven-step design procedure, and the two-layer (upper reinforced zone plus lower zone) settlement analysis (pp. 5-42 to 5-46).
sections.body: Section 4.2 covers rammed aggregate pier design: design considerations including stress ratio and replacement ratio (4.2.1), the design procedure (4.2.2) and settlement analysis by the two-layer approach (4.2.3) (pp. 5-42 to 5-46).
sections.applicability: Rammed aggregate pier design.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Rammed aggregate pier design is almost identical to stone columns; rammed stone has phi 45 to 50 degrees and higher stiffness; use a stress ratio of 5 to 10 under flexible embankments, about 10 under rigid footings, and a minimum replacement ratio of 0.33 (pp. 5-42 to 5-43).
sections.body: The design concept for rammed aggregate piers is almost identical to that for stone columns, and for area wide improvement the design method is identical (pp. 5-42 to 5-43). Stone compacted by impact ramming typically has a somewhat higher effective friction angle, 45 to 50 degrees, and potentially higher modulus, so the pier-to-soil stiffness ratio and design stress ratio should be higher than for stone columns (p. 5-43). Although the manufacturer's design manual suggests stress ratios of 20 or higher, a stress ratio of 5 to 10 for area improvement under flexible embankment loading appears warranted until more field data support a higher ratio. Under rigid footings a somewhat higher ratio (10) may be considered, with settlements and pier capacity computed from the loads on each element. The loads on pier and soil follow from the chosen stress and replacement ratios; the design area replacement ratio is set after evaluating the unimproved settlement, and a minimum of 0.33 is generally recommended (HITEC report, Collin 2007).
key_points: Rammed stone phi 45 to 50 degrees (p. 5-43).
Stress ratio 5 to 10 under flexible embankments; about 10 under rigid footings (p. 5-43).
Minimum area replacement ratio 0.33 (Collin 2007) (p. 5-43).
sections.applicability: Choosing stress and replacement ratios for rammed aggregate piers.

sections.title: Design Procedures
sections.summary: Seven-step embankment design process for rammed aggregate piers, parallel to stone columns; the major difference is the settlement analysis (pp. 5-43 to 5-44).
sections.body: Rammed aggregate piers are selected to increase bearing resistance, reduce settlement, increase shear strength or a combination (p. 5-43). The generalized embankment process is: (1) design without piers to find settlement and global stability and whether improvement is needed; (2) assume an area replacement ratio and column diameter; (3) determine spacing; (4) check pier load bearing resistance and revise diameter if needed; (5) determine total settlement of the embankment on piers; (6) check time rate of settlement, changing spacing if too slow (p. 5-44); (7) check global stability. The process is similar to stone columns; the major difference is the settlement analysis presented next.
key_points: Same seven steps as stone columns (pp. 5-43 to 5-44).
Settlement analysis is the main difference from stone column design (p. 5-44).
sections.applicability: Preliminary design sequence for rammed aggregate pier supported embankments.

sections.title: Settlement Analysis
sections.summary: Rammed aggregate pier settlement uses a two-layer approach (Lawton et al. 1994; Fox and Cowell 1998; Wissmann et al. 2002): total settlement s_tot = s_uz + s_lz (Eq. 5-11), upper reinforced zone plus lower zone (p. 5-44).
sections.body: Rammed aggregate pier settlement control design is based on a two-layer settlement approach described by Lawton et al. (1994), Fox and Cowell (1998) and Wissmann et al. (2002) (p. 5-44). The piers create a stiffened, engineered upper zone of reduced compressibility; settlement below the reinforced zone, the lower zone, is evaluated by conventional geotechnical approaches. The total settlement s_tot is the sum of the upper zone settlement s_uz and the lower zone settlement s_lz: s_tot = s_uz + s_lz (Eq. 5-11).
key_points: s_tot = s_uz + s_lz (Eq. 5-11, p. 5-44).
equations: Eq. 5-11: s_tot = s_uz + s_lz; total settlement as upper (reinforced) zone plus lower zone settlement
sections.applicability: Settlement of rammed aggregate pier supported embankments and structures.

sections.title: Settlement in the Rammed Aggregate Pier-Reinforced Zone
sections.summary: Upper zone: top-of-pier stress q_g = q [n_s / (n_s R_a - R_a + 1)] (Eq. 5-12) and s_uz = q_g / k_g (Eq. 5-13); n_s 4 to 45 for rigid footings, 5 to 10 suggested for embankments; k_g 75 to 360 pci for rigid footings (pp. 5-44 to 5-45).
sections.body: Settlement in the upper zone is estimated by first calculating the top-of-pier stress q_g = q [n_s / (n_s R_a - R_a + 1)] (Eq. 5-12), where q is the average applied bearing pressure, R_a the ratio of the cross-sectional area coverage of the piers to the matrix soil, and n_s the stress concentration ratio between piers and matrix soil (p. 5-44). Research shows n_s ranges from 4 to 45 for rigid footings; embankments and most MSE walls are not rigid, so ratios may be lower and should be chosen with care, with larger ratios at softer sites; 5 to 10 is suggested for settlement control of embankments (p. 5-45). The upper zone settlement is the top-of-pier stress divided by the pier stiffness modulus: s_uz = q_g / k_g (Eq. 5-13). Design stiffness modulus values range from 75 pci to 360 pci for rigid footings; conservative values should be used for embankments and transportation structures (Collin 2007).
key_points: n_s 4 to 45 for rigid footings; 5 to 10 suggested for embankments (p. 5-45).
k_g 75 to 360 pci for rigid footings; use conservative values for embankments (p. 5-45).
equations: Eq. 5-12: q_g = q [ n_s / (n_s R_a - R_a + 1) ]; top-of-pier stress (q = average applied bearing pressure, R_a = area coverage ratio, n_s = stress concentration ratio)
Eq. 5-13: s_uz = q_g / k_g; settlement of the rammed aggregate pier-reinforced (upper) zone, k_g = pier stiffness modulus
sections.applicability: Upper-zone settlement of rammed aggregate pier reinforced soil.

sections.title: Settlement below the Rammed Aggregate Pier Reinforced Zone
sections.summary: Lower zone settlement by elastic s_lz = dq H / E (Eq. 5-14) for cohesionless or overconsolidated soil or consolidation s_lz = c_c [1/(1+e_o)] H log[(p_o + dq)/p_o] (Eq. 5-15) for normally consolidated clay; stress influence factor by Westergaard, or 1.0 under embankments (pp. 5-45 to 5-46).
sections.body: Settlement below the reinforced zone is evaluated by conventional approaches: elastic analysis with Eq. 5-14 for cohesionless or overconsolidated cohesive soils, s_lz = dq H / E, and consolidation analysis with Eq. 5-15 for normally consolidated cohesive soils, s_lz = c_c [1/(1 + e_o)] H log[(p_o + dq)/p_o] (p. 5-45). H is the lower zone thickness, E the matrix soil elastic modulus, c_c the matrix soil coefficient of compressibility, e_o its void ratio, p_o the vertical effective stress at mid-layer and dq the average bearing pressure applied by the embankment, the applied pressure times the stress influence factor I_sigma. I_sigma can come from Boussinesq or Westergaard; Westergaard is typically used because pier-reinforced soil is layered, but for embankments I_sigma in the lower zone is typically taken as 1.0 because of their lateral extent (p. 5-46). Elastic approaches suit granular and heavily overconsolidated cohesive soils, with modulus from correlations to SPT N, undrained strength, CPT tip resistance or other in situ tests; consolidation approaches suit normally or lightly overconsolidated cohesive soils.
key_points: I_sigma typically 1.0 in the lower zone under embankments (p. 5-46).
equations: Eq. 5-14: s_lz = (dq H) / E; elastic settlement of the lower zone (cohesionless or overconsolidated cohesive soils)
Eq. 5-15: s_lz = c_c [1 / (1 + e_o)] H log[(p_o + dq) / p_o]; consolidation settlement of the lower zone (normally consolidated cohesive soils)
sections.applicability: Lower-zone settlement beneath rammed aggregate piers.

sections.title: Design Examples
sections.summary: Two worked examples: an embankment on soft clay over rock improved with rammed aggregate piers, and an embankment on soft clay over dense sand improved with stone columns using the Priebe curve (pp. 5-46 to 5-49).
sections.body: Section 4.3 (pp. 5-46 to 5-49) gives two design examples: settlement of an embankment over soft clay underlain by rock with rammed aggregate piers (4.3.1), and settlement of an embankment over soft clay underlain by dense sand with stone columns using the settlement ratio read from the Priebe curve (4.3.2).
sections.applicability: Worked settlement examples for aggregate column design.

sections.title: Rammed Aggregate Piers
sections.summary: Design example demonstrating the method to determine settlement of an embankment on soft clay over rock supported on rammed aggregate piers, with and without improvement (pp. 5-46 to 5-47).
sections.body: The first design example demonstrates the method to determine the settlement of an embankment supported on rammed aggregate piers (p. 5-46). It covers the problem statement, the settlement without ground improvement and the settlement with rammed aggregate piers.
sections.applicability: Worked example of rammed aggregate pier settlement.

sections.title: Problem
sections.summary: Example 1: 20 ft embankment (gamma 125) on 15 ft normally consolidated soft clay (gamma_sat 120 pcf, c_c 0.25, e_o 0.7, c_v 0.1 ft2/day) over rock; piers at 5 ft spacing, 2.75 ft diameter (p. 5-46).
sections.body: A new embankment is to be built over a soft clay layer underlain by rock (p. 5-46, Figure 5-24). As printed in Figure 5-24, the embankment is 20 ft high with gamma = 125 (printed 'psf'); the soft clay is normally consolidated, 15 ft thick, gamma_sat = 120 pcf, c_c = 0.25, e_o = 0.7, c_v = 0.1 ft2/day, with the water table at the ground surface. The task is to determine the total settlement after construction. The column spacing is 5 feet and the column diameter is 2.75 feet.
key_points: Embankment 20 ft, gamma 125; clay 15 ft, c_c 0.25, e_o 0.7 (p. 5-46).
Pier spacing 5 ft, diameter 2.75 ft (p. 5-46).
figures: Figure 5-24: Example problem 1 geometry.
sections.applicability: Input data for the rammed aggregate pier example.

sections.title: Total Settlement Magnitude without Ground Improvement
sections.body: Without ground improvement the effective stress at mid-clay is p_o = z (gamma_sat - gamma_w) = 7.5 ft (120 pcf - 62.4 pcf) = 432 psf, and the embankment load is q = gamma H = 125 pcf (20 ft) = 2,500 psf (p. 5-46). The consolidation settlement is S = c_c [1/(1 + e_o)] H log[(P_o + dq)/P_o] = 0.25 [1/(1 + 0.7)] (15) log[(432 + 2500)/432] = 1.83 ft = 22 inches (p. 5-47). The total expected settlement without ground improvement is 22 inches. The proposed column layout is shown in Figure 5-25 (s = 5 ft, n_s = 6, c_r = 2c_v, k_g = 65 pci).
key_points: Unimproved settlement 1.83 ft = 22 inches (p. 5-47).
equations: S = c_c [1/(1 + e_o)] H log[(P_o + dq)/P_o] = 0.25 (1/1.7)(15) log(2932/432) = 1.83 ft (p. 5-47); unimproved consolidation settlement

sections.title: Settlement Magnitude with Rammed Aggregate Piers
sections.body: With rammed aggregate piers (p. 5-47): the equivalent diameter is d_e = 1.05 s = 1.05 (5) = 5.25; the area ratio is R_a = A_g / a = 5.94 ft (printed unit; pier area) / (5.25 ft)^2 = 0.27; q = gamma H = 125 pcf (20 ft) = 2,500 psf. The top-of-pier stress from Eq. 5-12 with n_s = 6 is q_g = 2,500 psf [6 / (6(0.27) - 0.27 + 1)] = 6,383 psf. The upper zone settlement from Eq. 5-13 with k_g = 65 pci is s_uz = 6,383 psf / [(65 pci)(144 in2/ft2)] = 0.68 inches. The clay is underlain by rock, so this is the settlement worked in the example, compared with 22 inches unimproved.
key_points: q_g = 6,383 psf with n_s = 6 (p. 5-47).
s_uz = 0.68 inches with k_g = 65 pci (p. 5-47).
equations: R_a = A_g / a = 5.94 / (5.25)^2 = 0.27 (p. 5-47); area ratio in the example

sections.title: Stone Columns
sections.summary: Design example for an embankment on soft clay over dense sand improved with stone columns, using the Priebe curve settlement ratio (pp. 5-47 to 5-49).
sections.body: The second design example determines the settlement of an embankment over soft clay underlain by dense sand when supported on stone columns (pp. 5-47 to 5-49). It covers the problem statement, the unimproved settlement and the settlement with stone columns using the Priebe curve.
sections.applicability: Worked example of stone column settlement.

sections.title: Problem
sections.summary: Example 2: 15 ft embankment (gamma 125 pcf, 40 ft crest, 2H:1V slopes) on 50 ft soft clay (gamma_sat 120 pcf, e_o 0.6, c_c 0.2) over dense sand (N1_60 = 48); columns 3.0 ft diameter at 5.7 ft spacing; no settlement of the sand (pp. 5-47 to 5-48).
sections.body: A new embankment is to be built over a soft clay layer underlain by dense sand with an average N1_60 = 48 (p. 5-47). Figure 5-26 shows a 15 ft high embankment with gamma = 125 pcf, a 40 ft crest and 2:1 slopes, on 50 ft of soft clay (gamma_sat = 120 pcf, e_o = 0.6, c_c = 0.2) with the water table at the ground surface (p. 5-48). The task is to determine the total settlement after construction. The column spacing is 5.7 feet and the diameter 3.0 feet. No settlement of the dense sand is assumed.
key_points: Embankment 15 ft; clay 50 ft, c_c 0.2, e_o 0.6 (p. 5-48).
Column spacing 5.7 ft, diameter 3.0 ft (p. 5-48).
figures: Figure 5-26: Example problem 2 geometry and soils.
sections.applicability: Input data for the stone column example.

sections.title: Total Settlement Magnitude without Ground Improvement
sections.body: Without ground improvement (p. 5-48): p_o = z (gamma_sat - gamma_w) = 25 ft (120 pcf - 62.4 pcf) = 1,440 psf; q = gamma H = 125 pcf (15 ft) = 1,875 psf; and S = c_c [1/(1 + e_o)] H log[(P_o + dq)/P_o] = 0.2 [1/(1 + 0.6)] (50) log[(1,440 + 1,875)/1,440] = 2.26 ft = 27 inches.
key_points: Unimproved settlement 2.26 ft = 27 inches (p. 5-48).
equations: S = 0.2 [1/(1 + 0.6)] (50) log[(1,440 + 1,875)/1,440] = 2.26 ft = 27 inches (p. 5-48); unimproved consolidation settlement
sections.applicability: Baseline settlement for the stone column example.

sections.title: Settlement Magnitude with Stone Columns
sections.summary: Example 2 with stone columns: A/A_sc = (5.7)^2/(3.0)^2 = 3.6; the Priebe curve in Figure 5-27 gives a settlement ratio of 2.7, so the improved settlement is 10 inches (27/2.7) (pp. 5-48 to 5-49).
sections.body: With stone columns the area ratio is A/A_sc = (5.7)^2 / (3.0)^2 = 3.6 (p. 5-48). Using the Priebe curve in Figure 5-27 (after Wallays et al. 1983, the same chart as Figure 5-21 with the Priebe curve for phi = 37.5 degrees), the settlement ratio at A/A_sc = 3.6 is 2.7 (p. 5-49). The settlement of the embankment with stone column ground improvement is therefore 10 inches, i.e. the unimproved 27 inches divided by the settlement ratio. This is how the chapter applies the settlement improvement concept of Section 4.1.2.6: improved settlement = unimproved settlement / n.
key_points: Settlement ratio from the Priebe curve = 2.7 (p. 5-49).
Improved settlement 10 inches versus 27 inches unimproved (p. 5-49).
equations: A / A_sc = (5.7)^2 / (3.0)^2 = 3.6 (p. 5-48); area improvement ratio used to enter the Priebe curve
figures: Figure 5-27: Example problem 2 settlement ratio determination.
sections.applicability: Applying the Priebe settlement ratio to an embankment.

sections.title: Design Verification
sections.summary: Field verification by load tests and in situ tests must be specified: short-term, long-term and composite shear load tests; short-term tests to 150% of design load, 1 inch at 150-200% as acceptance; long-term group tests on 3 to 4 columns within 9 to 12; proof tests at 150-200%; modulus and bottom stabilization tests for rammed piers (pp. 5-49 to 5-51).
sections.body: A field verification program of load tests and in situ tests must be developed and specified regardless of contracting method (p. 5-49). Load tests before, during and after production verify design assumptions. Three types: (1) short-term tests for ultimate column bearing; (2) long-term tests for consolidation settlement; (3) horizontal or composite shear tests for composite strength for stability (p. 5-50). The short-term single column test is most common, run after construction pore pressures dissipate, with increments of about 10 percent of ultimate for slow loading or 20 to 25 percent for rapid loading, generally to 150% of design load; an acceptance criterion of 1 inch at 150 to 200 percent of design load is reasonable for columns supporting a structure. Mitchell (1981) reported area-load settlement 5 to 10 times the short-term single column test settlement, with little confirming data, so long-term tests on a minimum of three to four columns within a group of 9 to 12 at the proposed spacing are recommended, loaded over the tributary area until 90-95 percent consolidation. Proof tests during production apply 150 to 200 percent of the design load. CPT, DMT and PMT can measure lateral stress change, but long-term group tests are recommended instead (p. 5-51), with extensive in situ testing in the initial investigation. For rammed aggregate piers, a Modulus test and a Bottom Stabilization test are used for quality assurance (Collin 2007).
key_points: Three load test types: short-term, long-term, composite shear (p. 5-49).
Short-term increments 10% (slow) or 20-25% (rapid) of ultimate; to 150% of design (p. 5-50).
Acceptance: 1 inch at 150-200% of design load for structure support (p. 5-50).
Long-term: 3 to 4 columns within a group of 9 to 12, to 90-95% consolidation (p. 5-50).
Proof tests at 150-200% of design load (p. 5-50).
sections.applicability: Planning load tests to verify aggregate column design.

sections.title: Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Unless the agency has expertise with aggregate columns a performance specification is good practice; an experienced agency may use a method specification (p. 5-52).
sections.body: Like other specialty construction, unless the specifying agency has expertise in the design, construction and inspection of aggregate columns, it is good practice to specify the work under a performance type specification (p. 5-52). If the agency has the necessary experience with the technique, a method specification may be used. The section covers the performance specification, field inspection and improvement verification.
key_points: Performance specification unless the agency has aggregate column expertise (p. 5-52).
sections.applicability: Choosing the specification type for aggregate column work.

sections.title: Aggregate Column Performance Specification
sections.summary: A guide specification for aggregate columns was developed for GeoTechTools from 21 agency specifications (2 rammed piers only, 14 stone columns only, 5 both); its outline has Parts 1 General, 2 Equipment and Materials, 3 Execution, 4 Payment (pp. 5-52 to 5-53).
sections.body: As part of GeoTechTools, 21 specifications by state DOTs and other agencies were reviewed: two applied only to rammed aggregate piers, 14 only to stone columns and five to both (p. 5-52). They were used to develop the Guide Specification for Aggregate Columns, with commentary and instructions, available at GeoTechTools and applicable to both column types. Its outline: Part 1 General (1.01 Introduction, 1.02 Intent, 1.03 Standards and References, 1.04 Definitions, 1.05 Scope of Work, 1.06 Submittals, 1.07 Qualified Contractors, 1.08 Quality Assurance); Part 2 Equipment and Materials (2.01 Equipment, 2.02 Backfill Materials) (p. 5-53); Part 3 Execution (3.01 Site Inspection, 3.02 Aggregate Column Construction, 3.03 Performance Criteria, 3.04 Field Quality Assurance, 3.05 Rejection of Aggregate Columns, 3.06 Excavation of Column Tops and Utilities, 3.07 Subgrade Preparation, 3.08 Restrictions); Part 4 Payment (4.01 Method of Payment).
key_points: Guide specification developed from 21 agency specifications (p. 5-52).
Four parts: General; Equipment and Materials; Execution; Payment (pp. 5-52 to 5-53).
sections.applicability: Drafting an aggregate column performance specification.

sections.title: Field Inspection and Improvement Verification
sections.summary: Verification and detailed field inspection of aggregate column construction are very important but often neglected; thorough surveillance by Engineer and Contractor and good communication among all parties are essential (p. 5-53).
sections.body: Verification and detailed field inspection of aggregate column construction is a very important but often neglected aspect (p. 5-53). Thorough field surveillance by both the Engineer and the Contractor is essential, and good communication should be maintained at all times between inspection personnel, the Contractor, the Project Engineer and the Designer. Subsections cover stone columns, rammed aggregate columns and verification testing.
key_points: Thorough field surveillance by Engineer and Contractor is essential (p. 5-53).
sections.applicability: Organizing inspection of aggregate column construction.

sections.title: Stone Columns
sections.summary: Stone column QA: stone tests per 5,000 tons; stone consumption per 5 ft to estimate diameter; average diameter per 50 columns, none under 90% of minimum; verticality within 2 in. in 10 ft; free-standing amps plus 40; 100 ft acceptance zones; records; in situ tests between columns; ASTM D1143 load tests; location within 4 in. (pp. 5-53 to 5-55).
sections.body: A stone column QA program uses several methods (p. 5-53). Gradation, specific gravity, loose and compacted density tests are run on the stone at one test per 5,000 tons before construction. Column integrity depends on minimum diameter and compacted density; stone consumption (buckets of known weight or volume) is monitored with depth, and from loose and compacted densities the diameter can be estimated (FHWA 1983), with measurements at a maximum of 5-foot increments (p. 5-54). Decreased consumption may indicate caving or inadequate displacement. For any 50 consecutive columns the average diameter must meet the contract, and no column may be under 90% of the minimum diameter. No column axis should be inclined more than 2 inches in 10 feet. Each lift is re-penetrated to the specified amperage, as a minimum the vibrator free-standing current plus at least 40 amps. Large areas are divided into acceptance zones about 100 feet on a side. Records include column number, verticality, top and bottom elevations, buckets of stone, amperage with depth, times, obstructions and a digital log. Post-construction QA depends on application (p. 5-55): where densification is needed, SPT, CPT or PMT at central points between columns, with the same method before and after. In soft saturated clays, short-term load tests per ASTM D1143 after pore pressures dissipate, and longer-term tests over about one week on 3 to 4 columns within a group of 9 to 12 if settlement governs. No column should be more than 4 inches from its specified center. Post-installation gradation cannot be grounds for rejection under a method specification if other provisions were followed.
key_points: Stone tests: one per 5,000 tons (p. 5-53).

sections.title: Rammed Aggregate Columns
sections.summary: Rammed aggregate pier QC/QA: Bottom Stabilization (BSTA) tests, DCP testing with a 15 blows per 1.75 in. threshold, modulus tests (one per small project, 2 to 4 on larger, about one per 1,000 piers), uplift tests per ASTM D3689, location within 4 in., and daily installation reports (pp. 5-55 to 5-57).
sections.body: A rammed aggregate pier QC/QA program uses several methods (p. 5-55). The QC representative coordinates layout and elevations, observes installation, checks aggregate moisture, tests production piers and implements corrective measures. The Bottom Stabilization test (BSTA) re-tamps the pier bottom to verify displacement is acceptable (Collin 2007); a pattern of successful tests reduces it to spot checks (Fox and Cowell 1998) (p. 5-56). The Dynamic Cone Penetrometer verifies densification in the top few feet; if average resistance consistently exceeds 15 blows and less than 10% of tests fall below 15 blows per 1.75 inches, testing may be reduced to spot checks. Modulus tests, based on ASTM D1143, verify the stiffness modulus: typically one per small project, two to four on larger projects, and as a general rule one per 1,000 piers (Collin 2007). Uplift tests per ASTM D3689 verify tension performance, often run with the modulus test. Each pier center should be within four inches of plan. Daily reports record location, length and drilled diameter, planned and actual elevations, number of lifts and tamping time, average lift thickness, soil conditions, groundwater, unusual conditions and equipment. QA includes monitoring load test piers and tests, DCP testing and daily installation. Post-installation gradation testing cannot be grounds for rejection under a method specification if other provisions were followed (p. 5-57).
key_points: BSTA test verifies the stabilized pier bottom (p. 5-55).
DCP: average > 15 blows and < 10% below 15 blows per 1.75 in. allows spot checks (p. 5-56).
Modulus tests: 1 per small project, 2-4 on larger, ~1 per 1,000 piers (p. 5-56).
Pier center within 4 in. of plan (p. 5-56).

sections.title: Verification Testing
sections.summary: Verification testing differs for granular and cohesive soils; Table 5-1 (Esrig and Bachus 1991) ranks test suitability 1 to 5; small plate tests are fast but shallow, large plate tests use a plate equal to the column diameter, and zone loading tests apply up to 3 times design pressure over 4 to 9 columns (pp. 5-57 to 5-58).
sections.body: Testing of ground reinforced by aggregate columns should address the different response of granular and cohesive soils (p. 5-57). In situ tests suit soils where densification is expected; load tests suit those and mixed and cohesive profiles. Table 5-1 (Esrig and Bachus 1991) ranks suitability from 1 (least) to 5 (most), granular/cohesive: dynamic cone 2/1; mechanical cone 3/1; electric cone 4/2 (best test for seismic liquefaction evaluation); boreholes + SPT 3/2; dilatometer 3/1; pressuremeter 3/1; small plate load test 1/1; large plate load test 2/2; zone loading 4/4 (best for realistic comparison with foundations); full-scale 5/5 (rare). Short duration tests on 2-foot diameter metal plates are most common in Great Britain for speed and cost but stress only shallow depths and can be misread, particularly with residual pore pressures (pp. 5-57 to 5-58); in the United States large plate tests with the plate equal to the column diameter are typically used. Zone loading or dummy footing tests apply up to 3 times the design bearing pressure over a group of typically 4 to 9 columns, at significant expense. The loaded area must be large enough to stress the critical layer, normally the weakest cohesive layer of significant thickness, which governs the allowable load (p. 5-58).
key_points: Table 5-1 ranks tests 1 (least) to 5 (most suitable) (p. 5-57).
Electric cone 4 granular / 2 cohesive: best test for liquefaction evaluation (p. 5-57).
Zone loading 4/4: best realistic comparison with foundations (p. 5-57).
Zone load tests: up to 3x design pressure over 4 to 9 columns (p. 5-58).
Load must stress the critical (weakest significant cohesive) layer (p. 5-58).

sections.body: Section 6.0 gives guidelines for budget estimates of aggregate column feasibility (p. 5-59). Price depends on labor, stone price and availability, weather and environment, so experienced contractors should be contacted to verify budget and feasibility. Costs are typically a bid item measured by the lineal foot (LF) including material, equipment, labor and incidentals, with mobilization possibly paid separately. Table 5-2, Unit Costs (p. 5-60), from state DOT bid tabs 2007 through 2010: aggregate columns, greater than 1,000 LF, $20.00 to $60.00 per LF (typical $20 to $40); mobilization, 1 rig, $20,000 to $100,000 (high price for moderate depth rigs $40,000; increases beyond 500 miles; phased work may need multiple mobilizations); embankment, greater than 5,000 CY, use agency data; working platform geosynthetic, greater than 5,000 SY, $1.00 to $3.50; granular fill material, greater than 2,500 tons, $7.00 to $20.00. A working platform is often required and should be included when comparing technologies. The treatment area should consider loads transmitted on a 45-degree angle around the treatment zone perimeter, which extends the area to improve (p. 5-61). A preliminary budget spreadsheet is at GeoTechTools.

sections.title: Technology Used
sections.summary: Rammed aggregate piers saved 20 to 50% compared with deep foundation alternatives, allow spoil inspection, replace over-excavation or deep foundations, and allowed bearing pressures up to 10,000 psf (pp. 5-62 to 5-63).
sections.body: Rammed aggregate piers were a cost-effective solution, saving 20 to 50% compared with traditional deep foundation alternatives (p. 5-62). The method allows visible inspection of spoils and response to changing ground conditions, and is an effective replacement for massive over-excavation and replacement or for driven piles, drilled shafts or auger cast-in-place piles. The piers are formed by direct vertical ramming of successive lifts of high quality crushed rock into high stiffness elements; ramming also increases lateral stress and improves the surrounding soil (p. 5-63), giving settlement control and higher design bearing pressure, up to 10,000 psf.
key_points: Savings of 20 to 50% versus deep foundations (p. 5-62).

sections.title: The Construction Process
sections.summary: Installation by pre-augering a cavity (normally 5 to 30 ft deep) and ramming lifts of aggregate with a beveled tamper that densifies vertically and forces aggregate laterally into the sidewalls (p. 5-63).
sections.body: Installation uses pre-augering and vertical impact ramming energy (p. 5-63). A cavity is first drilled, normally about five to 30 feet deep depending on design; pre-drilling lets the soil between borings be seen. Aggregate is placed in lifts (Figure 5-28) and each lift is rammed with a patented beveled tamper, densifying the aggregate vertically and forcing it laterally into the cavity sidewalls, giving coupling with the surrounding soil and reliable settlement control.
key_points: Drill depths normally about 5 to 30 ft (p. 5-63).

sections.title: Solution
sections.summary: 1,411 rammed aggregate piers at 4 to 9 ft centers under walls 14 ft or higher raised bearing and global stability factors of safety above 2.0 and 1.3; base displacement under 1.5 in.; modulus test 0.69 in. at over 22,000 psf, more than twice the design stiffness (p. 5-64).
sections.body: A total of 1,411 rammed aggregate piers at spacings of four to nine feet on center were installed beneath wall heights of 14 feet or greater (p. 5-64, Figure 5-29). The factors of safety for bearing resistance and global stability were increased to greater than 2.0 and 1.3 respectively, and the piers allowed rapid pore pressure dissipation by radial drainage. Horizontal displacement at the wall base was measured at less than one and a half inches. The modulus test showed a total movement of 0.69 inches at a stress of more than 22,000 psf, indicating a pier stiffness greater than twice the assumed design value.
